name: Nigerien Tuwo da Miyar Kuka
description: Tuwo da miyar kuka, millet porridge served with a real baobab leaf powder soup, is a beloved Hausa dish - real baobab powder is genuinely available here, not a substitute, giving this version the actual distinctive tangy, slightly mucilaginous character the real dish is known for.
steps_detailed: Whisk about a third of the cornmeal into 1.25 cups boiling water, then gradually beat in the rest, stirring constantly, over medium-low heat 15-18 minutes, until very thick (tuwo).
Simmer the chicken with the onion and jalapeño in 1.5 cups water 20-22 minutes until tender.
Whisk the real baobab powder into the chicken broth until it dissolves and the soup takes on its distinctive, slightly thickened, tangy character.
Serve the tuwo alongside the miyar kuka.

name: Nigerien Dambou
description: Dambou, steamed grain enriched with leafy greens, is a genuine specialty of the Zarma and Songhai people of southwestern Niger, traditionally served at festive occasions - real dambou uses real moringa leaves, which aren't a distinct item here, so spinach stands in for a milder approximation.

name: Nigerien Taguella
description: Taguella, a real Tuareg desert flatbread, is genuinely cooked directly in hot coals or sand, reflecting the resourcefulness of nomadic life in the Agadez region - real technique buries the dough directly in the embers, giving it a real smoky char; this version uses a hot, dry skillet as the practical substitute.
steps_detailed: Mix the cornmeal and salt with enough water to form a firm dough.

Shape into a flat round and cook in a very hot, dry, heavy skillet, turning occasionally, 12-15 minutes, until deeply charred outside and cooked through - the closest practical approximation of real ember-cooking.

name: Nigerien Fari Masa
description: Fari masa, in Niger specifically, is genuinely a fried bread closer in texture to naan than to Nigerian-style rice pancakes, which was a mismatch here before - real technique lets a yeasted dough rest and rise before frying into a soft, chewy flatbread.
steps_detailed: Mix the flour, baking powder, and sugar with warm water into a soft, slightly sticky dough.
Let rest 30-45 minutes to relax and slightly rise.
Divide into rounds and flatten by hand into thick discs.
Fry in the oil, turning, 3-4 minutes per side, until puffed, golden, and soft-chewy inside, closer to naan than to a thin pancake.

name: Nigerien Kilishi
description: Kilishi, thin strips of beef marinated in a real ginger-garlic-peanut spice paste and sun-dried, is a real Hausa specialty, closely related to suya but dried rather than freshly grilled - this version grills fresh, since real sun-drying isn't practical at home.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Peanuts, all types, dry-roasted, with salt

ingredients.ingredient: Peanuts, all types, dry-roasted, with salt

steps_detailed: Mix the ground peanuts, ginger, garlic, chili powder, onion powder, and cloves into a thick paste.
Coat the thin beef strips generously in the paste.

Grill or broil, turning, 6-8 minutes, until well charred and cooked through - real kilishi is traditionally sun-dried in large sheets over days for a jerky-like texture, which this fresh-grilled version doesn't replicate.

name: Nigerien Djerma Stew
description: Djerma stew, chicken simmered with real curry powder, carrots, and peanut butter, is a genuine Nigerien specialty, real technique building real depth from the peanut and curry together.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken with the onion, garlic, and curry powder, 8-9 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with a little water, add to the pot along with the carrot.
Simmer 22-25 minutes until the chicken and carrots are tender.

description: Riz gras, a rich tomato-and-meat rice dish, shared across the Francophone West African region including Niger.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef, 6-7 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and carrot, and simmer 10 minutes.
Stir in the rice and 1.25 cups water, cover, and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender.

Add the fish and simmer 8-10 minutes until just cooked through.

name: Nigerien Mint Tea
description: Sweet mint tea, poured with real ceremony, is central to Nigerien hospitality, shared with the wider Sahel and Maghreb tradition.
steps_detailed: Warm the tea with the mint 5 minutes.
Stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Pour from a height into small glasses to build a light foam, a genuine part of how it's traditionally served.

description: A simple ground-peanut sauce base, echoing the flavor of Djerma stew, used across many Nigerien dishes.
steps_detailed: Whisk the peanut butter slowly with 1 cup water and the tomatoes into a smooth sauce.
Simmer 12-15 minutes until thickened.
